chapter: Army service and the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
title: Arrival at Camp Funston, the sergeant's slap and the typing test
summary: White describes the slap at the gate, reporting to the major, and being picked out for office work and then for musicians.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: New Mexico. But anyhow, it's cold up around there. Well, I finally reached Camp Funston on one of these old slow trains, but it looked like they didn't care how you traveled in those days, you see, army movements. I reached Camp Funston along about two o'clock in the afternoon. Maybe it might have been a little earlier than that, but anyhow, when I got to the gate, I had my trumpet with me and I had a little bag. I had an extra pair of shoes there, an extra pair of pants. I don't know why I carried them along. I knew I was going to need them. I didn't think so anyhow. But anyhow, just to be ready for an occasion. And the sergeant at the gate said to me, where is the sheriff who brought you here? I told him, I said, no sheriff brought me here. Yes, you did. Where is the man who brought you here? And he kept on asking me. I said, no man brought me here. And what I said, and I said kind of forcibly, I said, I came unguarded here. He slapped me. And I didn't say nothing. I just took the little slap and I kind of halfway grinned. But brother, all the hell and fury had gotten into me then. If I must go to war, don't beat me up before I get in there. All right.
So he pushed me down through the gate. Go on in there.

I went in the gate and I went straight on up the step. Now, my plan of action is already in me. I know what to do because I've had a little military training in the schools. They taught us military training in James. They also carried some drill tactics in Benedict and all the colleges down there. They didn't have no regular ROTC.

Go ahead. But the order of the day had to be obeyed in the colleges and in the schools all through the South. When I got in, I asked for the officer in charge. So they referred me to a major over there who afterwards became one of my majors, Major Blaine. And I saluted, came to attention and I had no training but I knew this had to be done. And I said, sir, I'm Private Amos Mordecai White reporting from Nevada, Missouri. I was arrested two days ago for not having my card on me. I had the card and I came here unguarded. Sheriff Dawes granted me that privilege because he saw I wanted to get in the Army. I have no near relatives to which my paper could be sent that I might have received them. So I, the best thing for me to do is to have my mail sent en route with the circus because I'm on the Cole Brothers' circus this season. And I said, as I came in the gate, the officer, the non-commissioned officer at the gate slapped me and kicked me and beat me up at the gate. I put it all in straw. He said, said to his orderly, go to the gate and bring that sergeant at the gate here. I brought this tall sergeant at Gawkes Camp from Georgia. And he says, that's Sergeant Major. He says, come here. He called him over to me. He snatched the chevron off first. I'm about, Sergeant Major, what's that? He says, for kicking and hitting this man at the gate. While he's trying to give you an explanation for coming into the service. Take him to the guardhouse and put him in there and lock him up and throw the key away until I tell you when to pick it up. And I laughed. And I said, ha, ha, ha. And when I laughed, the Major told me, shut up. And stand at attention. Yes, sir. I don't even know for my mouth. Well, he sent me into the D-cootie. I had no more than got my uniform on and delivered to me. I didn't even have them strapped to the legs around me or anything. When they called me, said, fall out! Fall out! Line out! Any of you fellas here? Of you crutes? This is old Sergeant Clark talking now. Know how to type right? I said, me! Step us two paces forward. Sent me to the office. I got there, start picking at the type right. I could type correctly, but I couldn't type faster. I had no keyboard back. Printing, you see the case on the printing case is almost similar. But any man who can print correctly and observe punctuations and capitalizations, you can type you don't let them better than one of these half-handed, ill-tuted supposed secretaries. Well, I typed out a letter for him. Typed it out quicker than anybody in there, too. My nervous self. That's good, sir.

They dismiss me out. Go to your barracks. I'll go over to the YMCA. Fall out again in a half an hour. Next time, fall in! I'm out again. How many of you men in here have had any office work experience? Me. I had experience in everything. But the last call they issued around about six o'clock. You know, the sun's way up. How many musicians are in this rank?
